title: Support graceful reassembly of partial UTF-8 sequences and delimited records in streamed structured output
creator: Aisha Rahman
description: Users have reported corrupted JSON when clients resume or retry streaming sessions and chunk boundaries split multi-byte UTF-8 characters or when endpoints must interoperate with older clients that expect line-delimited JSON (LDJSON). This ticket scopes a compatibility and repair layer in the streaming path to: (1) detect and repair partial UTF-8 sequences that span chunk boundaries, (2) support an optional lightweight LDJSON compatibility mode for legacy clients, and (3) add an idempotent retry token and minimal manifest/header so retries can resume without producing duplicate or corrupted records. The goal is to make streaming structured outputs robust across network truncation, client retries, and cross-version client/server combinations while bounding memory and latency overhead.
reproduction_steps: Start a streaming generation that emits UTF-8 multi-byte characters (e.g. emojis, accented scripts) inside JSON string values.
Force a TCP-level truncation so one stream chunk ends in the middle of a multi-byte UTF-8 codepoint (simulate via proxy that cuts bytes).
Client attempts to resume from last received byte using an application-level retry; observe invalid UTF-8 sequences or JSON parse errors on the client side.
Repeat with an older client that treats each newline as a complete record (LDJSON); stream contains embedded newlines in string values or uses envelope framing, causing deserialization mismatch.
proposed_solutions: Byte-level boundary scanner in the server chunker that identifies valid UTF-8 codepoint boundaries and ensures we only cut at safe offsets; emit boundary metadata for the client to use when resuming.

If safe cut is not possible within latency SLO, emit a small escapement byte sequence (e.g. a 1-2 byte sentinel) and include its mapping in the stream header so old clients can understand fallback behavior.

Optional LDJSON compatibility mode: provide a toggle on the response (response header: X-Redwood-Stream-Mode: ldjson) where the runtime converts envelope JSON into one-line records and escapes internal newlines predictably. Include a version marker so legacy clients can detect behavior.

Idempotent retry token: attach a short monotonic segment id in a per-request manifest (Segment-Id + Resume-Offset) so retries are reconciled server-side and duplicates are suppressed in the reassembly layer.

Repair heuristic for resumption: on resume attempt, server compares client resume-offset and uses the byte-backtracking decoder to align to last valid UTF-8 boundary; then replay from the next safe boundary with an overlap window to validate idempotence.
Memory safety: cap reassembly buffer to 64KB per active stream; if exceeded, fail fast with a clear error and guidance for clients to re-initiate a fresh request with the manifest id.
design_decision: Implement server-side UTF-8 boundary-aware chunker + optional LDJSON compatibility toggle. Provide a per-request manifest header (X-Stream-Manifest) containing stream mode, segment id, and graceful-resume policy. Add idempotent retry reconciliation to prevent duplicates. Chosen because it keeps client changes minimal and centralizes correctness in the runtime with bounded resource use.
acceptance_criteria: Streaming responses never cut in the middle of a UTF-8 codepoint when stream mode is 'default'; verified by fuzz tests covering multi-byte sequences across 10K random cut positions.
Clients using the resume protocol succeed resuming without JSON parse errors in both default and ldjson modes in >99.9% of simulated network truncations.
LDJSON compatibility toggle produces one record per newline for legacy clients and documents escaping rules; integration tests validate roundtrip parsing with the legacy parser implementation.
Idempotent retry token prevents duplicate records: replay acceptance tests show no duplicated logical records after 1-3 retry sequences.
Runtime memory usage for reassembly is capped and observed to be under 64KB per stream in load tests (95th percentile).
API docs updated and migration guide published (Confluence + SDK changelog).
test_plan: Unit tests: byte-level boundary scanner, backtrack-to-valid-utf8 algorithm, manifest header parsing.
Integration tests: simulated truncated TCP streams at arbitrary byte offsets across 50K test cases including emojis, CJK, and combining diacritics.
Compatibility tests: run legacy LDJSON client emulator against new toggle to verify parseability and escaped-newline semantics.
Chaos tests: introduce packet loss and late retries to ensure idempotence and correct overlap window behavior.
Performance tests: measure additional latency introduced by boundary checks at 95th and 99th percentiles under baseline load.
rollout_plan: Feature gated behind runtime feature flag: stream_utf8_boundary_repair=false by default.
Deploy server-side implementation to canary pool (10% of traffic) with detailed tracing enabled for segment ids and boundary adjustments.
Monitor canary for 48 hours; if no parsing errors or SLO regressions, enable on 50% traffic and run another 72-hour validation.
Enable globally and flip default to true after 7 days of stable metrics; post-mortem if any regression observed.
Publish SDK patches that add optional resume logic to recommend clients use manifest header for robust resume.
monitoring_metrics: stream.resume_success_rate: percent of resume attempts that complete without parse errors
runtime.latency_delta_ms_95: added latency due to boundary scanning
stream.reassembly_buffer_oom: count of streams hitting 64KB cap
compat.ldjson_parse_failures: failures reported by LDJSON compatibility mode

notes: This approach centralizes stream robustness in the runtime instead of forcing all clients to implement byte-level recovery. Keep an eye on tail latency; fallback is to provide a short escapement sequence for hard cut cases to avoid visible corruption when operating in strict SLO modes.
